items.title: Drill: twenty mixed
items.prose: Twenty mixed questions at the 80-in-8 pace: 6 seconds each, two minutes in all. Time yourself with your own watch and write your time down. Afterwards, mark which ones were slow.
items.question: Fill in all twenty answers.

feedback.correct: All twenty right. Compare your time with two minutes, and note the slow kinds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows, then log which kind each slip was.

explain.text: The set mixes every move of this level: left to right, cross multiplication and shortcuts, estimate and correct, and moving the point. A row that took far over 6 seconds names your next drill. Repeat the set later in the week and compare times.

items.title: Pace and score in code
items.prose: `pace_needed(score, seconds=120)` is the seconds an answer a score needs. `score_at(pace_by_op, mix, seconds=120)` takes each kind’s mean seconds and its share of the questions (shares add to 1), and returns the score as a whole number of answers. Kinds missing from `mix` do not count.
items.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: three paces (compared with math.isclose) and seven scores, including the lesson’s 40, 53, 41 and 44, a mix with only two kinds, and an 8-minute round. Scores must be whole numbers.

feedback.correct: Both functions match the lesson’s scores.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each kind by its share, then floor 120 divided by the pace.

explain.text: The pace is the share-weighted mean of the times, and the score is the whole number of answers that fit. Looping over `mix`, not `pace_by_op`, leaves out kinds the test does not ask. `math.floor` turns 53.3 into 53.

items.title: An error report
items.prose: Log entries are `(question, op, seconds, first_try_right)`. `make_log(seed)` builds a seeded 30-answer round, already defined. For each op, report the mean seconds, the error rate (wrong first tries over answers) and the share of all the seconds. Then pick the op to drill first by this rule: if any op’s error rate is 0.25 or more, the op with the highest error rate; otherwise the op with the largest share of time.
items.question: Complete `error_report(log)`, returning `(report, drill)` with `report[op] = (mean, error_rate, share)`.

widget.prelude:
import random
RULES = {  # op: (min s, max s, chance the first try is wrong)
    'add': (1.5, 3.0, 0.05),
    'sub': (1.5, 3.0, 0.25),
    'mul': (2.5, 5.0, 0.08),
    'div': (2.5, 7.0, 0.08),
}
SYM = {'add': '+', 'sub': '−', 'mul': '×', 'div': '÷'}
def make_log(seed, n=30):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    log = []
    prev = None
    while len(log) < n:
        op = rng.choice(['add', 'sub', 'mul', 'div'])
        if op in ('add', 'sub'):
            a, b = rng.randint(2, 100), rng.randint(2, 100)
            q = f'{a} + {b}' if op == 'add' else f'{a + b} − {a}'
        else:
            a, b = rng.randint(2, 12), rng.randint(2, 100)
            q = f'{a} × {b}' if op == 'mul' else f'{a * b} ÷ {a}'
        if q == prev:
            continue
        prev = q
        lo, hi, pw = RULES[op]
        s = round(rng.uniform(lo, hi), 1)
        wrong = rng.random() < pw
        if wrong:
            s = round(s + rng.uniform(1.5, 3.0), 1)
        log.append((q, op, s, not wrong))
    return log

tests.call: {k: tuple(round(x, 4) for x in v) for k, v in error_report(make_log(50))[0].items()}
{k: tuple(round(x, 4) for x in v) for k, v in error_report(make_log(51))[0].items()}
{k: tuple(round(x, 4) for x in v) for k, v in error_report(make_log(52))[0].items()}

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: the report and the drill for `make_log(50)`, `make_log(51)` and `make_log(52)` (values rounded to 4 places), three short logs, and a check that the shares add to 1.

feedback.correct: The rule picks division for seed 50, multiplication for 51 and subtraction for 52.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the error rate threshold, 0.25, and that shares use all the seconds in the log.

explain.text: Seed 51 has no kind wrong a quarter of the time, so share of time decides: multiplication, 38% of the round, though division has the higher mean. Seed 52 flags subtraction, wrong 2 times in 7, before its speed. Accuracy first, then the biggest share of time.

items.title: Cross multiplication, step by step
items.prose: Put the working for $76 \times 58$ in order. Each line carries its reason. One line drops a carry: leave it out.
items.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.why: You dropped the carry. 86 tens are 8 hundreds and 6 tens, so add 860.

feedback.correct: Three terms in any order, then the cross added with its carry, then the units.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the three terms before you add.

byKey.d1: You dropped the carry. 86 tens are 8 hundreds and 6 tens, so add 860.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the dropped carry belongs.
byKey.o4: Add the cross once both it and the hundreds are worked out.

explain.text: The three terms are 35 hundreds, 86 tens and 48. Adding left to right gives 3,500, then 4,360, then 4,408. Dropping the 8 hundreds from the cross would give 3,608.

items.prose: Size the answer, then estimate and correct.
items.question: What is $7{,}488 \div 36$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Three digits: try 200 first.

byKey.lost-zero: You lost the zero in the tens: $36 \times 28 = 1008$.
byKey.point: 2.08 is a hundred times too small.

explain.text: $36 \times 100 = 3600$ and $36 \times 1000 = 36000$, so three digits. 200 lots make 7,200, and $288 = 36 \times 8$. There are no tens, so the middle digit is 0: 208.

items.prose: A fund charges 0.125% on a £48,000 subscription. Note that 0.125 is $\tfrac18$.
items.question: What is the charge, in pounds?

feedback.correct: 1% is £480, and an eighth of it is £60.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find 1%, then take an eighth of it.

explain.text: 1% of £48,000 is £480. 0.125% is $\tfrac18$ of 1%, and $480 \div 8 = 60$. So the charge is £60.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the whole part, then divide the remainder by 13.

byKey.remainder: You wrote remainder 6 as 0.6. It is $\tfrac{6}{13}$, about 0.46.

explain.text: $13 \times 38 = 494$ leaves 6. $6 \div 13$: 60 tenths give 4 with 8 left, 80 hundredths give 6. So 38.46.

items.title: Your error analysis
items.prompt: The table holds a seeded warm-up round (seed 54): 30 answers before the bell. “wrong” means the first answer typed was wrong. Write an error analysis of this round as if it were your own. (a) Find each kind’s mean seconds and share of the time, and name the slowest. (b) Sort the wrong first tries into slips and method gaps, with a reason for each. (c) Write a one-week plan that uses the daily warm-up on Today and a targeted drill. (d) Say how you will know the plan worked.
items.model:
**1. Where the time went.** The 30 answers took 110.5 seconds, and the bell cut off a 31st.

| Kind | Answers | Mean (s) | Share of time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Addition | 7 | 2.57 | 16% |
| Subtraction | 6 | 2.83 | 15% |
| Multiplication | 9 | 4.36 | 35% |
| Division | 8 | 4.54 | 33% |

Division has the highest mean, 36.3 seconds over 8 answers. Multiplication takes the largest share: 39.2 of 110.5 seconds, because there were 9 of them.

**2. Errors.** Five first tries were wrong. Subtraction was wrong 2 times in 6 (33%), multiplication 2 in 9 (22%), addition 1 in 7 (14%), division never. The five wrong rows took 25.7 seconds between them.

- $6 \times 2$ wrong (5.9 s): a slip, since it is a table fact.
- $83 - 50$ wrong (4.7 s): a slip; no method is needed.
- $68 + 96$ wrong (4.3 s): a carry slip.
- $110 - 73$ wrong (4.3 s): a method gap. Crossing 100 needs counting up: 27 to 100, then 10, so 37.
- $6 \times 58$ wrong (6.5 s): a method gap. Splitting gives $300 + 48 = 348$.

**3. What to drill first.** By the homework's rule, subtraction is wrong a third of the time, so accuracy comes first. Then multiplication by splitting, which has the largest share of time, then division.

**4. A one-week plan.** Each day, about 15 minutes:

1. Three minutes of subtractions that cross 100, counting up, aloud.
2. Four minutes of one-digit by two-digit products by splitting, then three of divisions by estimate and correct.
3. Five warm-up rounds from Today, noting each score.

On days 6 and 7, drop the separate drills to two minutes and keep the five rounds.

**5. How I will know it worked.** The baseline is a score of 30. I compare the average of each day's five rounds, not the best one, with that baseline. At the end of the week I log one round again in the same table and check two numbers: subtraction errors near zero, and multiplication under 3.5 seconds. As a target, multiplication at 3 seconds and division at 3.5 would bring the 30 answers to 90 seconds: a pace of 3 seconds, so a score of 40.

rubric.text: Gives the four means (about 2.57, 2.83, 4.36 and 4.54 seconds) and names division as slowest by mean.
Gives shares of time and notes multiplication takes the largest share (about 35%).
Counts the wrong first tries per kind and flags subtraction, wrong 2 times in 6.
Sorts the five errors into slips and method gaps with a reason for each.
Plans a week with daily warm-up rounds and drills aimed at the flagged kinds, drilled alone and then mixed.
Judges progress by an average of many rounds against the baseline, and re-logs a round to check.
